intended_object: Take a finite family b : ι → M (in practice a spanning family) and let π : R^ι → M be the map w ↦ Σ wᵢ bᵢ. A matrix A ∈ M_ι(R) represents an endomorphism f of M when π ∘ A = f ∘ π, i.e. f(b_j) = Σ_i A_ij b_i for every j. This is the matrix representation used in the Cayley–Hamilton / determinant-trick argument for finitely generated modules (Atiyah–Macdonald 2.4). I took this from the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
The definition requires `fromMatrix R b A = fromEnd R b f`. By the `_apply` lemmas in the same file, the left side is w ↦ linearCombination b (A *ᵥ w) and the right side is w ↦ f (linearCombination b w). So the condition says exactly π ∘ A = f ∘ π, the textbook condition. Evaluating at the standard basis vectors turns it into f(b_j) = Σ_i A_ij b_i.

The setting is already the natural one. `R` is an arbitrary commutative ring; commutativity is needed so that a matrix acts R-linearly on ι → R and for `algEquivMatrix'`. `M` is an arbitrary module and `ι` is any finite type. No spanning hypothesis is built into the definition; that hypothesis appears only in the lemmas that use it. Fintype ι is needed for the finite sums in the linear combination.

The library has no other, more general definition of this notion. Mathlib's `LinearMap.toMatrix` assumes a basis, so it is a more special notion rather than a generalisation of this one.
